subtype: Approach: thinking what would spoil the game and blocking it [Thinking]
passage: Saturday night. Nikita and I made up a hide-and-run game today on the school field. Before we started I asked us both: what could ruin this? Two things came up. One, if the hiding spots are unlimited, the seeker will search all day. Two, if there are no edges, people will run off to the road. So we fixed a limit of two minutes for hiding and drew a boundary in chalk around the big tree and the swings. We tested it three times and it was great. I wish I could always ask that question first. Devika.

qa.q: What limit did Devika and Nikita set for hiding?
qa.a: They set a limit of two minutes for hiding.

qa.q: Why did Devika ask what could ruin the game?
qa.a: Devika worried the game could become unfair or endless, and wanted to prevent problems before playing.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Devika use if problems still appear, and why?
qa.a: Devika could run a short trial round and change the rules that do not work. Playing shows problems that thinking may miss.

qa.q: How might Nikita see the two-minute rule?
qa.a: Nikita agreed to the limit and the chalk boundary, so it probably felt like a fair rule that made the game more exciting for a hider as well as a seeker.

grounding: Devika asks what could make the game unfair or dull and prevents it with a hiding time limit and a chalk boundary.
